  3. Choose scope and download — Pick 'All pages' or 'This page only' and click 'Crop & Download' to get the result.

Crop PDF — Drag and resize the box, crop and download — on your device, free. Open the tool

Does cropping delete content?

No. Cropping is a standard PDF operation that narrows the page's visible area (CropBox); the remaining area displays and prints cleanly. It runs entirely in your browser, and your file is not sent to a server.

To crop different areas on different pages, use 'This page only' and apply it page by page. If you need to rotate pages first, use the 'Rotate PDF' tool.

Cropping is not deleting — and that has a consequence

Cropping narrows a page's visible area; the trimmed part is not removed from the file, only hidden. For everyday use that distinction does not matter, and the document looks as you want on screen and in print. It becomes critical if you crop in order to hide information: the text in the cropped area stays in the file and can technically be restored. When something genuinely has to go, you need a tool that removes content permanently.

Where it helps most on scans

Scanners work to the paper size, so an A5 receipt scanned on A4 leaves half the page blank. Reading such a document means constant scrolling, and in print the small content sits marooned in the middle of a large sheet. Trimming the margins makes the document both readable and tidy, and pages look consistent when you merge several receipts.

Getting the order right before cropping

  • Rotate sideways pages first; the crop box works relative to page orientation.
  • Delete unwanted pages first, leaving fewer pages to crop.
  • With mixed page sizes, applying one crop to all of them can cut content on some.
  • If you will add page numbers, leave them until last — the number is placed relative to the new edge.

What happens in print

A cropped page reaches the printer as a smaller page, and the printer may enlarge it to fit the sheet. That usually makes the text more legible and is often exactly what you want. But if the document must be a specific size on paper — an official form, for example — cropping changes that size. On such documents it is worth thinking twice.

Does file size change?

Because cropping does not remove content, file size does not drop meaningfully. If size is your problem, you need compression rather than cropping. Using both makes sense: narrow the page to the area you want, then compress the file.

item.title: How to Convert a CV (Résumé) From Word to PDF the Right Way
item.dc:creator: PDF Platform
item.description: Why you should send your CV as a PDF for job applications, and how to convert it from Word without breaking the formatting — step by step.
item.content:encoded:
A CV is the first document an employer sees about you. A résumé built in Word can shift on different computers and its fonts can change. The fix is simple: convert it to PDF before sending.

Why should a CV be sent as a PDF?

  • Looks the same on every device: Fonts, line spacing and layout are preserved regardless of who opens it.
  • Professional standard: Most employers and career portals prefer, or even require, PDF.
  • Won't change by accident: A Word file can shift when opened; a PDF is fixed.

Convert a Word CV to PDF — step by step

  1. Upload your Word file — Drag and drop your .doc or .docx résumé into the Word-to-PDF tool.
  2. Convert — Click "Convert"; the PDF is prepared instantly with fonts, tables and layout preserved.
  3. Download and name it — Download the PDF and save it with a clean name like "First_Last_CV.pdf".

Convert Word to PDF — Upload your résumé and download it as a PDF without breaking the formatting — free. Open the tool

Final checks before you send

  • Is the file name professional? Use "First_Last_CV.pdf" instead of "document1.pdf".
  • Do the fonts and alignment in the PDF match the Word version?
  • Are the photo and links (LinkedIn, email) in the right place?
  • If the file is too big, shrink it to email size with "Compress PDF".

If you're asked to send several documents (CV + cover letter + certificates) as one file, convert them to PDF and then combine them with "Merge PDF".

How application systems read your CV

At most large employers and career portals your CV is read by software first, and reaching human eyes depends on that. These systems parse the text in the document, so your PDF must contain real text. A CV exported as an image from a design tool, or built from a screenshot, is a blank page to the system. There is a simple test: open the PDF and try to select your name with the cursor; if you cannot, it is an image.

Layouts that make automatic reading harder

  • Two-column designs: reading order can scramble and details run together.
  • Burying information in text boxes or tables.
  • Putting contact details in the page header — some systems never read headers.
  • Showing skill levels only as bars or stars; information with no text equivalent is not recorded.
  • Unusual section headings; a creative title instead of «Experience» makes matching harder.

Cleaning up on the way from Word to PDF

A PDF freezes the Word document as it stands, so before converting you should turn off track changes, accept all revisions and delete comments — otherwise those traces can end up in the output. Review the author name in document properties too; if you took the template from someone else, another name may still be sitting there.

File name and sending

A recruiter downloads dozens of files a day, and a document called «cv_final_v3.pdf» gets lost in the folder. A name in the form First_Last_CV is easier to find and looks considered. When a cover letter and certificates are requested, merging them into one PDF is tidier than separate attachments, and page numbers show the document arrived complete.

A last look before sending

  • Do fonts and alignment look the same as in Word?
  • Are links (LinkedIn, portfolio) clickable and pointing at the right address?
  • Is the file size reasonable — compress it if a photo inflated it?
  • Is there an old employer name or a draft note left in that you did not want shown?
  • Open it on a phone once; many recruiters take their first look there.

item.title: How to Fill Out a PDF Form Online for Free (Flat Forms Too)
item.dc:creator: PDF Platform
item.description: No need to print and hand-fill a PDF form you received. Whether it has fillable fields or not, here's how to add text and sign a PDF — step by step.
item.content:encoded:
Applications, contracts, petitions... Most PDF forms are actually "flat" — they have no ready fields you can click and type into. Instead of printing and filling by hand, you can add text directly on top of the form.

There are two kinds of PDF forms

  • Fillable (interactive) form: It has ready fields; you can click and type into them in any PDF reader.
  • Flat form: Most official/scanned documents are like this; there are no ready fields. Here you add text "on top" at the right spot.

Filling a flat PDF form — step by step

  1. Upload the form — Upload your PDF form to the annotate/text tool.
  2. Add text — With the text/note tool, click the relevant blank and type your answer; add a separate box for each field.
  3. Sign and download — If needed, add your signature and download the filled PDF with "Apply & download".

Add Text/Markup to PDF — Upload your form, add text to the blanks, and download the filled PDF — free. Open the tool

If a signature is required

If the form asks for a signature, after adding your text you can draw/type your signature and place it. Signing happens entirely on your device; your document is not sent to a server.

For checkboxes, add a small "X" or "✓" text. If the form has multiple pages, add text/marks to each page separately.

Which kind of form do you have? Find out in thirty seconds

Which method you need depends on the form, and finding out is easy: open the PDF and click a blank. If a cursor blinks and you can type, the form is fillable; if nothing happens, it is flat. On fillable forms, filling the fields directly is the cleanest route because the text sits inside the field and aligns itself. On flat forms you place text on top of the page instead.

Accented characters in fillable forms

Some PDF forms are built with a limited character set, so letters outside it can disappear or turn into question marks when typed. That is the form author's font choice rather than a mistake by whoever fills it in. Reading the fields back once after filling is the practical way to catch this.

What locking the form does

When you send a fillable form, its fields are still editable; the recipient can change one without noticing, or the form may appear empty in a different program. Locking the fields makes what you typed a permanent part of the page, so the document looks the same everywhere. On an official application this step ensures the form arrives complete and unaltered.

Alignment on flat forms

  • Set the text size close to the line height; oversized text spills onto the neighbouring line.
  • Use a separate text box for each field; one long line breaks the alignment.
  • A small mark is enough for a checkbox — do not overflow the box.
  • Where day/month/year have separate boxes, type into each one separately.
  • Check at 100% zoom before downloading; text that looks right at screen scale can shift in print.

Signing and sending

Most forms ask for a signature. Adding yours after filling and sending the document as one file is tidier and easier for the recipient than sending separate pages. If the other side must sign too, sending the document out for signature by email and keeping a record of the process is the safer route.

A final check before sending

Are all required fields filled, is the date in the requested format, and are the requested attachments included? Those three questions prevent most applications from coming back. Keeping a copy of the completed form is also worth it, and removes the later question of what you wrote.

item.title: iLovePDF Alternative: Free PDF Tools, File Stays On Device
item.dc:creator: PDF Platform
item.description: The key question when looking for an iLovePDF alternative: where does my file go? An honest comparison with tools that run on-device, need no signup and add no forced watermark.
item.content:encoded:
iLovePDF is popular, but for most operations your file is uploaded to its servers first. When you're handling a sensitive contract, ID or financial statement, that leaves a question mark. Here's how to do the same tasks without your file ever leaving your device.

Where does your file go in iLovePDF?

In most online tools like iLovePDF, merging, splitting or converting uploads your file to a server, processes it there, and then deletes it. It's usually safe, but the file still goes to the internet for a while. For confidential documents, the safest approach is for the file to never leave your device.

What to look for in an alternative

  • Privacy: Is the file uploaded to a server, or processed in your browser?
  • Forced watermark: Is a stamp added to the free output?
  • Signup requirement: Does a simple task require an account?
  • Daily/usage limits: How many operations can you do for free?

The PDF Platform difference: structural tools run on-device

On PDF Platform, structural operations like merge, split, rotate, delete pages, reorder pages and image-to-PDF run entirely in your browser (on your device) — your file is never sent to the internet. No signup is required, no forced watermark is added to the free output, and it even works when your connection drops.

Merge PDF — Add your files, reorder and download one PDF — on your device, free. Open the tool

Which tools run on-device, which on the server?

To be honest, not every operation can run in the browser. Here's the clear split:

  • On-device (file never leaves): merge, split, rotate, delete pages, reorder pages, image → PDF, document scan, sign and annotate.
  • On the server (content not stored, encrypted connection): Word/Excel/PowerPoint conversion, OCR, compression and AI tools (summarize, chat, translate).

If you only need to merge or split a confidential document, pick the on-device tools; your file never touches the internet. If conversion is needed, content is not retained after processing.

What iLovePDF does well

A comparison is only useful if it is honest. iLovePDF has been doing this for a long time and does it well, so you should know what you would be giving up:

  • Years of track record and mature infrastructure.
  • Desktop and mobile apps — you are not limited to a browser.
  • Very broad language support and a large user base.
  • Developer tooling for organisations that need it.

If what you need is a desktop program or an enterprise-scale setup, staying where you are may well be the better call. We run in the browser and have no separate desktop app.

Which one should you pick?

There is no single right answer — it depends on what you are doing.

  • If the document is sensitive (a contract, an ID, a medical report, customer data) and the job is page-level editing: pick the on-device tool. A file that is never uploaded beats a promise to delete it later, every time.
  • If you want a desktop program: we run in the browser, so look elsewhere.
  • If you only process a few files now and then: the free plan is enough, and with no watermark you can use the result as-is.
  • If you work with Turkish documents: the interface, the OCR and the AI tools treat Turkish as a first language rather than a translation layer added afterwards.

Test the claim yourself

You do not have to take "your file stays on your device" on trust. You can check it in thirty seconds:

  1. Open the merge tool — No account needed. Pick a couple of PDFs you want to merge.
  2. Disconnect from the internet — Turn off Wi-Fi or unplug the cable. Do not reload the page.
  3. Run the merge — It completes and you download your file. If it works with no connection, your file is not going anywhere.

item.title: Free PDF Editor: Add and Delete Text, Sign and Fill Forms
item.dc:creator: PDF Platform
item.description: There's no single way to edit a PDF: changing text, adding text, signing, annotating... A guide to which tool to use for what you actually need.
item.content:encoded:
"Editing a PDF" means different things to different people: some want to change existing text, some to add notes on top, some to sign. Pick the right tool and it takes seconds. Here's a roadmap by need.

1) Change or delete existing text

If you want to actually remove text in a PDF and type new text, use the "Edit PDF" tool. Draw a box over the text to change, type the new text (leave empty to delete) and download.

Edit PDF — Truly delete and replace existing text — draw a box, type the new text, download. Open the tool

2) Add text, notes or marks on top

To add text, highlights, boxes or drawings on top without touching existing text, the "Annotate PDF" tool is ideal. You can also use it to fill in blanks on forms.

3) Sign

To sign a document, use the "Sign PDF" tool to draw, type or upload your signature and place it anywhere on the page. Signing happens entirely on your device.

4) Fill forms

For forms with no fillable fields (flat), you can fill them by adding text directly on top — see our form-filling guide for detailed steps.

For confidential documents, annotating and signing run entirely on your device; your file doesn't go to a server. Real text deletion/editing is done on a secure server and the file isn't stored after processing.

Ask the right question first: what do you want to edit?

«Editing a PDF» is not one job; it is a shared name for several similar-looking jobs with different results. Picking the wrong tool makes the task look impossible or produces an unexpected outcome. Four questions separate what you need:

  • Are you changing text in the document? — you need text editing.
  • Are you adding your own notes? — markup is enough.
  • Are you arranging pages (delete, reorder, merge)? — page tools.
  • Are you removing information permanently? — redaction; markup or cropping will not do.

What to watch for in free tools

A tool offered free usually charges somewhere else, and it is worth seeing where before you start. The common patterns: a watermark on the output, a daily or hourly limit, your document uploaded to a server, a mandatory account before download, and reduced quality in the downloaded file. Checking those five points while trying a tool keeps you from getting stuck mid-task.

Before you start editing

The type of document largely decides what you can do. In a PDF with a text layer you can change the text; in a scan the page is an image and needs converting to text first. If the document is password-protected, no tool can read its content until the password is removed. Those two checks answer most of the «why is it not working?» questions upfront.

Common scenarios and the right order

  • Changing a clause in a scanned contract: convert to text first, then edit.
  • Turning several documents into one file: merge, then reorder, then add numbers last.
  • Cleaning a document before sharing: delete unneeded pages, redact sensitive data, clear metadata.
  • Filling and returning a form: fill, sign, lock, and compress if needed.

The limits of editing

Text in a PDF does not flow; replacing a word with a longer one does not reflow the line. For small corrections that is no problem, but if paragraphs will be rewritten, producing the document from its source or converting to Word is less work. The test is simple: a few words means edit directly, pages of rewriting means convert.

item.title: Convert Word to PDF Without Breaking Formatting
item.dc:creator: PDF Platform
item.description: Converting your Word file to PDF before sharing guarantees the layout looks the same for everyone. Here's the most practical way to go from Word to PDF without breaking formatting.
item.content:encoded:
When you send a Word document, a different Office version or a missing font on the other end can shift your layout. PDF fixes this: the document looks identical for everyone. Here's how to convert Word to PDF without breaking formatting.

Why convert Word to PDF?

  • Locks the layout: fonts, tables and spacing look the same everywhere.
  • Opens on any device: phone, tablet, computer — no special software.
  • Can't be edited by accident: safe for proposals, contracts and CVs.
  • Official submissions usually require PDF.

Step by step

  1. Upload the document — Drag your .doc, .docx, .odt or .rtf file into the Word to PDF tool.
  2. Convert — The document is processed on the server and converted to PDF with layout, fonts and tables preserved.
  3. Preview and download — Check the result and download the PDF. The page structure matches your original document.

Word to PDF — Convert your Word document to PDF with layout intact. Open the tool

Tips for preserving formatting

If your document uses standard fonts (Arial, Times New Roman, Calibri), the output will be closest to the original. Very custom, non-installed fonts may render differently on some systems.

Need the other direction — turning a PDF back into an editable Word file? We have a separate tool for that.

PDF to Word — No editable version on hand? Convert the PDF back to Word. PDF → Word

Prepare the document before converting

A PDF freezes the Word document as it stands, so whatever is in the file ends up in the output. A few minutes of preparation prevents surprises you would otherwise notice after sending.

  • Turn off track changes and accept all revisions, or the markup can end up in the output.
  • Clear comments, especially leftovers from internal review.
  • Run the spell check once; fixing it in a PDF is far harder.
  • Update the automatic contents page and field codes, or old page numbers get frozen in.
  • Review the author and company details in document properties.

Why fonts shift

A Word file usually does not embed its typefaces; it only records their names. If the font is not installed on the other end, the program substitutes something similar, line lengths change, tables overflow and even the page count differs. A PDF embeds the fonts it uses. That is PDF's most useful property, and it explains why official submissions ask for it.

A note on CVs and applications

Documents sent with job applications are often uploaded into a system and scanned automatically, so it matters that the text inside the PDF is real text. A document produced straight from Word satisfies that; a CV exported as an image from a design tool or captured as a screenshot does not. There is a simple test: open the PDF and try to select your name with the cursor. If you cannot, the document is an image.

Checklist after converting

  • Is the page count as expected, or did an extra blank page appear?
  • Are tables split across a page break?
  • Is there an unwanted break between a heading and its text?
  • Did links stay clickable?
  • Does the file size fit the channel you are sending through?

What you can do afterwards

Once you have the PDF you can keep working on it: merge it with annexes, add page numbers, reduce its size or permanently remove sensitive details. Most of these operate at page level, so they leave the content and appearance of the document untouched.

item.title: How to Convert Excel to PDF Keeping Tables and Layout (2026)
item.dc:creator: PDF Platform
item.description: Sending an Excel file as-is often results in shifted cells and broken page layout. Here's how to convert Excel to PDF while keeping tables intact and print-ready.
item.content:encoded:
Sending an Excel table often ends with shifted columns, split pages and a broken print area on the other end. PDF fixes this: the table looks identical and print-ready for everyone. Here's how to convert Excel to PDF without breaking the layout.

Why convert Excel to PDF?

  • Locks the layout: cells, column widths and page breaks look the same everywhere.
  • Print-ready: print-area and fit-to-page issues disappear.
  • Can't be changed by accident: safe for report, quote and invoice tables.
  • Opens on devices without Excel installed.

Step by step

  1. Upload the Excel file — Add your .xls, .xlsx, .ods or .csv file to the Excel to PDF tool.
  2. Convert — The file is processed on the server and converted to PDF with tables, cells and formatting preserved.
  3. Preview and download — Check the result and download the PDF — your table is share- and print-ready.

Excel to PDF — Convert your Excel table to PDF with layout intact. Open the tool

Tip for wide tables

For wide, many-column tables, setting the page orientation to Landscape and adjusting the print area in Excel before converting helps everything fit and stay readable.

The reverse: getting a table out of a PDF

If you have a PDF and want to edit the table inside it in Excel, we have a separate tool that extracts tables to .xlsx.

PDF to Excel — Export tables from a PDF into editable Excel. PDF → Excel

Set the print options before converting

What the resulting PDF looks like is decided by the print settings in the file. A wide table converted without them comes out with columns scattered across pages and is unreadable. A couple of minutes of setup completely changes how usable the output is.

  • Set orientation to landscape: with many columns this is almost always needed.
  • Define the print area to stop empty cells spreading across pages.
  • Use the «fit all columns on one page» option.
  • Set the header row to repeat on every page — it decides readability on multi-page tables.
  • Decide whether gridlines should print.

Files with several sheets

An Excel file usually holds several worksheets, and not all of them need sharing. When working calculations, raw data or old period tabs end up in the output, the document both bloats and can carry information that was never meant to leave. Deciding which sheets go into the output before converting is cleaner than deleting pages from the PDF afterwards.

Watch for hidden information

Excel files carry more than they show: hidden rows and columns, data concealed by filters, cell notes and other sheets that formulas point at. Hidden rows usually stay out of the PDF, but cell notes and filtered data can appear unexpectedly. Reviewing everything hidden before converting a table that is going outside is a good habit.

For invoice and quote tables

The real reason for converting quotes and invoices prepared in Excel is to create a fixed document whose figures the recipient cannot change. Two extra steps help when sending it: page numbers show completeness on multi-page quotes, and a permissions password restricts copying and editing.

Before you send the output

  • Do page breaks fall in sensible places, or is a line item split in half?
  • Do amounts and currency display correctly?
  • Is the smallest type readable, especially if it will be printed?
  • Is there a note or column left in that you did not want shown?
